title: Washington Crossing the Delaware: every mistake, every face, and the river that is really the Rhine
question: A flag that didn't exist yet, a boat too small, a river in Germany. What else did the painter get wrong, on purpose?

secondary: who is in washington crossing the delaware
seo.meta_title: Washington Crossing the Delaware: Mistakes and Hidden Details
seo.meta_description: A guided zoom through Leutze's Washington Crossing the Delaware (1851): the anachronistic flag, the small boat, James Monroe, the crew, and the Rhine.

intro: Washington Crossing the Delaware is a painting by the German-American artist Emanuel Leutze from 1851, now in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. It shows George Washington standing in a small boat among ice floes on the night of 25 to 26 December 1776, on his way to the surprise attack at Trenton. It is one of the most famous images of American history, and it is full of things that could not have happened: the flag, the boat, the light, even the river.

sections.heading: Christmas night, 1776
paragraphs: On the night of 25 to 26 December 1776, Washington led the Continental Army across the icy Delaware River and attacked the Hessian troops at Trenton, New Jersey, the next morning. The victory came at a desperate moment in the American Revolution.
The crossing took place in the dark and in bad weather. The boats Washington used were large cargo boats, 40 to 60 feet long, carrying soldiers, artillery and horses.

sections.heading: Painted in Germany, for Europe
paragraphs: Leutze, a German-American painter working in Düsseldorf, conceived the painting during the Revolutions of 1848. He hoped the example of the American Revolution would encourage Europe's liberal reformers. He painted it in Düsseldorf, using American tourists and art students as models and assistants, among them the painter Worthington Whittredge. The river in the background is the Rhine.
His first version, from 1850, was damaged by fire in his studio, restored, and bought by the Kunsthalle in Bremen. It was destroyed in a British bombing raid on 5 September 1942.

sections.heading: A sensation in New York
paragraphs: The second, full-size version was shown in New York in October 1851. More than 50,000 people came to see it. The businessman Marshall O. Roberts bought it for $10,000, and in 1897 John Stewart Kennedy gave it to the Metropolitan Museum.

Its huge gilded frame is a replica, made in 2011 from an 1864 photograph by Mathew Brady. A smaller third version, which hung in the White House from 1979 to 2014, sold at Christie's in May 2022 for 45 million dollars.

sections.heading: What Leutze got wrong
paragraphs: The flag is an early version of the Stars and Stripes, which was only specified by Congress on 14 June 1777 and first flown that September, months after the crossing. The boat is far too small: real Durham boats were much bigger, and the army's cargo boats could carry horses and cannon. The crossing happened at night, not under a golden sky.
And Washington standing up? It looks reckless, but the historian David Hackett Fischer argues that everyone would have stood, to keep out of the icy water sloshing in the bottom of the boat.

meaning: Leutze was not painting a documentary. He was painting a symbol: a nation crossing from defeat to victory, led by a calm, upright Washington into the light.

The crew makes the same point. Leutze filled the boat with different kinds of Americans, from a western rifleman to farmers, a Scot, a man of African descent and a figure dressed like a Native American: a whole country in one boat, pulling together. For an audience in revolutionary Europe in 1848, that was the message.
whereToSee: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York. Check the Met's website before you visit.

details.headline: Christmas night, 1776
details.text: The American army is losing. Washington gambles: cross the icy Delaware in the dark and attack at dawn. Leutze painted the moment 75 years later, with a few liberties.

details.headline: Washington
details.text: At the centre, standing tall, one foot forward, cloak blowing: Washington, the only calm man in the boat.

details.headline: A face in the light
details.text: Look at his face. The sky behind him is unnaturally bright, and his profile catches the first light of the morning. Leutze lit the hero like a stage.

details.headline: Mistake one: the flag
details.text: The Stars and Stripes didn't exist yet. Its design was specified in June 1777, six months later.

details.headline: And holding the flag?
details.text: According to the 1853 exhibition catalogue, it is Lieutenant James Monroe, the future fifth president of the United States.

details.headline: At the bow
details.text: In front, a man in a fur cap and green coat pushes the ice away with his pole: a western rifleman.

details.headline: Look at the crew
details.text: Behind him, a man in a Scottish bonnet and, beside him, a man of African descent. Leutze filled the boat with all kinds of Americans.

details.headline: Holding on to his hat
details.text: In the middle of the boat, a man clutches his hat against the wind: General Edward Hand, according to the traditional identifications.

details.headline: Farmers in the boat
details.text: Next to him, men in broad-brimmed hats, one with a bandage around his head. Ordinary farmers, turned soldiers.

details.headline: At the stern
details.text: At the back of the boat, a figure in fringed clothes, dressed like a Native American, steers with the oar.

details.headline: Mistake two: the boat
details.text: The real boats were much bigger. Washington's army crossed in cargo boats 40 to 60 feet long, with cannon and horses. This one would barely hold its crew.

details.headline: Horses in the background
details.text: Behind them, other boats carry horses and more soldiers. Those horses could never have fitted in a boat like Washington's.

details.headline: Ice
details.text: All around, blocks of ice drift past, painted so they glitter. The crossing was cold, wet and dangerous.

details.headline: Mistake three: the light
details.text: They really crossed in the dark and in foul weather. But in the sky here, a single star still shines over a dawn that had not come yet.

details.headline: And that river?
details.text: Leutze painted it in Düsseldorf, Germany. The water and the hills behind them belong to the Rhine.

details.headline: But one 'mistake' isn't
details.text: People say no one would stand in a boat like that. Historians say they all stood: the bottom was full of icy water.
